Tibial plafond fractures may result from low-energy trauma (rotational injury) or, more
frequently, high-energy trauma (falls, motor vehicle collisions).
They represent life-altering injuries with a guarded prognosis.
Appropriate initial management is crucial to prevent early complications.
Definitive surgical management includes biologic, accurate open reduction of the articular
surface, restoration of length and alignment, stable fixation, and appropriate postoperative
wound management.
Surgical treatment options must be tailored to the patient and the fracture (definitive external
fixation and internal fixation options exist).
Various postoperative complications can occur.

Overview
Tibial plafond fractures are some of the more challenging orthopaedic injuries to
manage given the injury complexity and patient outcomes associated with the injury.
After several decades of poor surgical outcomes, attention to the substantial soft-tissue
injury that often is associated with tibial plafond fractures has resulted in staged
management. The initial stage is designed to stabilize the soft tissues with the use of a
provisional external fixator with possible fibular fixation and to obtain CT scans to better
understand the articular fragments and aid in surgical planning. The final stage focuses
on achieving anatomic articular reduction and correcting length, alignment, and rotation
of the distal tibia while respecting the soft-tissue envelope. Postoperative complications,
including infection, nonunion, and posttraumatic osteoarthritis, may drastically affect
patient recovery. Patient rarely return to pre-injury levels of activity.
Epidemiology
A plafond/pilon fracture is a distal tibial fracture with articular surface involvement.
Tibial plafond/pilon fractures account for less than 10% of lower extremity injuries.
The mean patient age is 35 to 40 years.
More common in males than females
The most common mechanisms of injury include motor vehicle collisions and falls from height;
injury generally results from an axial load of the talus on the plafond.

Epidemiology
Tibial plafond/pilon fractures are distal tibia fractures with associated injury to the tibial
articular surface of the ankle joint. Plafond, which is the French term for ceiling, refers to
the articular tibial surface as the roof of the ankle joint (Figure 1). Another term for tibial
plafond fractures, pilon fracture, is derived from the French term for a pestle, which is
used with a mortar to grind or pulverize substances. Tibial plafond fractures commonly
affect younger male patients in their thirties and forties. The most common mechanism
of injury of tibial plafond fractures involves an axial load to the distal tibia, which typically
is observed in patients who sustain a fall from height or are involved in a motor vehicle
collision. Although tibial plafond fractures account for less than 10% of all lower
extremity fractures, the incidence of tibial plafond fractures is increasing. This likely is
related to better safety mechanisms at the workplace and in automobiles that prevent
patients from death but allow them to sustain the lower extremity injury.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The ankle joint is relatively constrained because of the overall osseous congruence of the
tibia, talus, and fibula (Figure 1). The tibial plafond is rectangular in shape and forms the
roof of the ankle joint. The talus is wider anteriorly than posteriorly, which creates the
relative stability during weight bearing but allows for flexibility during plantar flexion.
The medial malleolus is located on the medial aspect of the distal tibia and is larger
anteriorly than posteriorly. The distal fibula forms the lateral restraint to the ankle joint.
Ligamentous support on the medial and lateral aspects of the ankle provides additional
stability during rotation. Laterally, the anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior
talofibular ligaments provide a restraint to inversion injury. Medially, the deltoid
ligament consists of the deep and superficial fibers to resist external rotation. The
superficial fibers pass from the anterior colliculus to the navicular, sustentaculum tali,
and medial talus. The deep fibers originate on the posterior colliculus and insert on the
non-articular aspect of the medial talus. The deep deltoid is the principal stabilizer of the
talus in the ankle mortise. The syndesmosis is a collection of ligaments, including the
anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL), posterior-inferior tibiofibular ligament
(PITFL), transverse ligament, and interosseus ligament. The syndesmotic ligaments
maintain the relationship of the fibula within the tibial incisura and play a role in
maintaining ankle stability during external rotation. Knowledge of AITFL and PITFL
anatomy and insertions is critical because they insert on the Chaput and Volkmann
fragments, respectively. Transection of these ligaments must be avoided during the
approach and reduction of the Chaput and Volkmann fragments. In addition, adequate
stabilization of these fragments during definitive fixation is critical to avoid a
syndesmotic equivalent injury that may lead to poorer patient outcomes.1
The muscular and tendinous anatomy is important to understand because it may aid in
maintaining anatomic planes during the surgical approach. The anterior compartment
consists of the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, and
peroneus tertius. The deep peroneal nerve runs within the anterior compartment. The
superficial posterior compartment consists of the gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris,
which join to form the Achilles tendon. The deep posterior compartment consists of the

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Axial compression (high-energy injury; ie, fall from height)
The force is directed axially through the talus into the tibial plafond, causing impaction of the
articular surface; may be associated with considerable comminution (Figure 3).
If the fibula remains intact, the ankle is forced into varus with impaction of the medial
plafond (Figure 4).
Plantar flexion or dorsiflexion of the ankle at the time of injury results in a primarily posterior
or anterior plafond injury, respectively (Figure 5).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most tibial plafond fractures result from a high-energy mechanism of injury, such as a
fall from height or a motor vehicle collision. The axially directed force drives the talus
into the tibial plafond, which creates the multi-fragmentary fracture that may include
joint impaction and comminution. More of the anterior or posterior plafond may be
involved if the foot is in dorsiflexion or plantar flexion on impact, respectively (Figure 5).
The classic tibial plafond fracture consists of a posterolateral Volkmann fragment, an
anterolateral Chaput fragment, central joint impaction, and a medial malleolus fragment
(Figure 8). Although most patients with a plafond fracture have an associated fibular
fracture, substantial risk for varus collapse is present in patients who have a fracture
with an intact fibula (Figure 4).

Low-energy tibial plafond fractures tend to result from torsion in combination with
coronal plane stress in a varus or valgus position (Figure 6). This scenario creates larger
fracture fragments that tend to be associated with relatively simple fracture patterns
and little articular disruption. Patients with a low-energy tibial plafond fracture likely
have a better prognosis given the lower energy nature of the injury and the limited
impact to the joint surface. Patients who sustain a combined compression and shear
mechanism of injury may have a fracture pattern with joint impaction and simple
fracture extension into the metadiaphyseal or diaphyseal tibia (Figure 7).
Risk Factors
Tibial plafond/pilon fractures may result from a twisting injury while participating in an activity
such as snow skiing.
Tibial plafond/pilon fractures may result from a high-energy axial load through the ankle.
Accidents, such as motor vehicle collisions and falls from height, may result in a tibial pilon
fracture.

Risk Factors
Tibial pilon fractures may result from various mechanisms of injury. The important
distinction is whether the mechanism of injury is a low-energy or high-energy
mechanism of injury. The difference in energy absorbed by the leg will guide definitive
management. A substantial twisting injury to the lower extremity may result in a spiral
tibia fracture that extends into the tibial plafond. This is the mechanism of injury
involved in snow skiing or similar accidents. The soft-tissue and osseous injuries are of
moderate intensity. Other mechanisms of injury involve high-energy accidents, such as
falls from a considerable height, motor vehicle collisions, or any accident involving a

Associated Injuries
Compartment syndrome is rare after a tibial plafond fracture.
Vascular injury may occur but is associated with questionable clinical consequences.
Posteromedial neurovascular structures or tendons may become entrapped (Figure 2).
Ipsilateral talus and/or calcaneus fractures are rare.
Syndesmotic injury is relatively common, occurring in 15% of patients with a plafond fracture.

Associated Injuries
Compared with injuries of the proximal and midshaft tibia, tibial plafond fractures rarely
are associated with compartment syndrome. Prior series have reported a zero to 5%
incidence of compartment syndrome in patients with a tibial plafond fracture.2-4 More
recently, a series on 708 tibial plafond fractures reported a 2.8% incidence of
compartment syndrome. The series identified male sex, fracture extension from the joint
surface, zone of comminution, and bone loss as substantial predictors for compartment
syndrome.1
Vascular injury is surprisingly common in patients with a tibial plafond fracture. In a
consecutive series of 25 patients with a tibial plafond fracture, LeBus et al5 reported that
vascular injury was identified via CT angiography in 52% of the patients. The most injured
vessel was the anterior tibial artery (nine patients). One-half of the vessel injuries were
complete occlusions; however, a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse was noted in all the
patients. In addition, no increased rates of infection or wound complications were
reported in the patients with vascular injury.
Preoperative assessment of axial CT scans is critical to identify entrapment of
posteromedial structures in patients with a tibial plafond fracture. In a series of 420
plafond fractures, Eastman et al6 reported an entrapped posteromedial soft-tissue

structures. The neurovascular bundle was entrapped in four patients (10%). A separate

Given that the typical mechanism of injury involves a motor vehicle collision or a fall
from height, patients with a tibial plafond fracture typically have some associated
injuries. Some series have reported major organ system injury in 27% to 51% of patients
with a tibial plafond fracture.3,7-9 However, ipsilateral calcaneus fractures and/or talus
fractures are rare in patients with a tibial plafond fracture.10,11
Ankle syndesmotic injury has been thoroughly studied in patients with a rotational ankle
fracture; however, ankle syndesmotic injury has been reported to occur in 15% of
patients with a tibial plafond fracture. A missed syndesmotic injury may result in rapid
joint deterioration and posttraumatic osteoarthritis.1 Syndesmotic-equivalent injuries
(small fractures involving the Chaput or Volkmann fragment at the location at which the
AITFL or PITFL insert) are more common than purely ligamentous injury in patients with
a tibial plafond fracture. Haller et al1 recommended syndesmotic fixation for the
management of tibial plafond fractures with a Chaput or Volkmann fracture fragment
that is 10 mm or smaller.
Injury Classification
No universally accepted classification of tibial plafond/pilon fractures exists.
Important characteristics to consider include articular and metaphyseal comminution,
shortening of the tibia resulting in proximal displacement of the talus, impaction of individual
or multiple joint fragments, associated soft-tissue injury, and vital structure entrapment in
fracture fragments.
Various fracture patterns may result, depending on the position of the foot and the precise
direction and magnitude of the force applied

Injury Classification
In classifying a tibial pilon fracture, the osseous and soft-tissue injuries must be
considered. Classification systems are used for two purposes. First, the classification
system should be able to guide management, including patient prognosis. Second the
classification system should aid in comparing the efficacy of various treatment options

for similar fracture patterns. The two most common fracture classification systems used
for tibial pilon fractures (the Rüedi-Allgöwer classification system and the OTA/AO
Foundation classification system) are based on the radiographic studies. The Rüedi-
Allgöwer classification system includes three categories, in which the severity of injury
increases from type I to type III. The Rüedi-Allgöwer classification system is of historical
importance and is not used in current clinical practice. In the OTA/AO Foundation
classification system, the tibia is designated as a 4 and the distal tibia is designated as a
3. Therefore, tibial pilon fractures are classified as a 43. Type A fractures are extra-
articular fractures. Type B fractures are partial articular fractures. Type C fractures
involve substantial intra-articular injury. Each fracture type is subdivided into three
groups (1, 2, or 3). As the energy imparted to the bone increases, the comminution and
the subcategory increase. Therefore, a 43-C3 injury is much more severe than a 43-A1
injury. In addition, the patient prognosis is substantially worse. Most surgeons do not
use osseous classification systems in the routine management of tibial pilon fractures.
The morphology of the articular injury and the extent to which the injury extends
proximally into the tibial shaft are important to determine. This is defined based on
findings observed on CT scans. Leonetti and Tigani12 presented a new classification
system for tibial pilon fractures based on CT scans. The authors reported that this
classification is treatment-oriented, prognostic, reliable, and reproducible; however, this
system has not yet become widely used.
An understanding of the severity of soft-tissue injury is of equal importance. The
Tscherne classification system is used for closed injuries, and the Gustilo-Anderson
classification system is used for open injuries. The Tscherne classification system and the
Gustilo-Anderson classification system are include three categories with increasing stage
corresponding with increasing soft-tissue damage secondary to injuries of progressively
increasing severity. Tscherne grade 3 injuries must be managed with greater caution. If
internal fixation is going to be performed, the timing of surgical management is crucial to
decrease the risk of wound healing and infectious complications. No incisions should be
made until the soft tissues have adequately recovered. For extensive soft-tissue damage,
external fixation should be considered as a definitive treatment option.
Open fractures are classified according to the Gustilo-Anderson system. This system
classifies open fractures as grade I, grade II, or grade III. Grade III injuries are

A final classification to consider is the classification of posterior tibial pilon fractures,
which occasionally are identified as posterior malleolus fractures. These are injuries that
are more severe than most rotational ankle fractures but not as severe as plafond/pilon
fractures caused by an axial load. Posterior tibial pilon fractures are posterior malleolus
fractures that extend from the posterolateral malleolus to the posteromedial malleolus.
The complexity of posterior tibial pilon fractures must be recognized, and posterior tibial
pilon fractures must be managed appropriately to improve functional outcomes.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Determine if mechanism of injury was high energy or low energy
Determine all associated medical comorbidities
Determine if the patient has symptoms of other orthopaedic injuries
Determine if evidence of injury to other body systems is present.
Determine if any numbness or tingling indicating a nerve injury is present

Patient History
The patient history, including the mechanism of injury, is extremely important. A patient
with a lower energy injury will have different clinical findings and different associated
injuries compared with a patient with a higher energy injury. A thorough review of
systems is essential to rule out associated injuries, such as intra-abdominal or neurologic
injuries. A patient history should include associated orthopaedic and neurovascular

affect the outcome of the management of the tibial pilon fracture. Diabetes mellitus is
one of the most important comorbidities. The surgeon should determine if an existing
neuropathy present and the level of glucose control.
Physical Examination
A thorough trauma survey of entire body must be performed.
An assessment of the stability and alignment of the ankle joint is useful. The orientation of the
ankle is observed, including its length, alignment, and rotation.

Most tibial pilon fractures are managed surgically because articular displacement cannot

tolerated over the next 2 to 4 weeks. Serial radiographs are essential to ensure adequate
maintenance of alignment. Physical therapy is initiated after cast removal to advance
weight bearing and to improve range of motion and strengthening.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Internal fixation
General
Internal fixation of high-energy tibial plafond fractures via definitive plate fixa­tion continues
to evolve.
Initial successes with this technique, described by Rüedi and Allgöwer, were fol­lowed by
many reports of failure, with the incidence of wound complications approach­ing 40% in a
large series of patients with a high-energy tibial plafond fracture.
Staged management via early external fixation with or without fibular fixation followed by
definitive reduction and fixation after soft-tissue healing has reduced the rate of wound
complications to zero to 6%,
Definitive internal fixation typically is performed in two stages.
Stage 1—Fibular plating to regain lateral column length and application of a simple spanning
external fixator. Two proximal half pins are placed on the anterior tibia (Figure 14).
Placement of pins within or outside the zone of future surgical management is
controversial and has not been definitively shown to affect complication rates.
A 5- or 6-mm centrally threaded pin can be placed across the calcaneus and attached to the
proximal half pins with the use of a combination of struts. This technique is simple to
perform and maintains stability and alignment. Extra care is necessary to avoid pressure
from bony fragments on soft tissues, prevent shortening, and maintain forefoot
positioning.
Typically, a delay of approximately 2 weeks is necessary to allow the soft tissues to heal.
Stage 2—Formal articular reduction and internal fixation
After ORIF is performed, incisions are made only as large as required to ana­tomically reduce
the articular surface. Periosteal stripping is performed only at the edges of the fracture to
achieve visual­ization of the reduction while preserving the blood supply.
Pre-contoured plates may be useful; anteromedial and anterolateral plates facilitate
percutaneous placement.
Bone graft or substitutes to fill metaphyseal voids was previously described as a standard
step in the fixation of a tibial plafond fracture; however, with less extensive dissection in the
metaphyseal region, grafting has become less routine.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Internal fixation has become the mainstay of the definitive management of tibial plafond
fractures. Respect for the surrounding soft-tissue envelope is paramount and drives the
decision to proceed with single- versus two-stage surgical management. Given that most
patients with a tibial plafond fracture sustained a high-energy injury and have a tenuous
soft-tissue envelope, a two-stage surgical fixation strategy typically is used to manage
tibial plafond fractures.
Staged management of acute tibial plafond fractures has become the standard of care
for most high-energy fractures given the reduced complication rates via this
technique.18,19 Although some literature supports early, definitive fixation, this
approach should be used sparingly based on careful patient selection and leg soft-tissue
evaluation.21
Open fractures require thorough evaluation and planning to adequately eliminate
foreign contamination and débride devitalized tissue that may serve as a host for future
infection. Frequently, these open wounds occur along the medial aspect of the distal
tibial metaphysis and are associated with tension failure along the medial side with
valgus presentation of the tibial plafond. These injuries warrant extension of the
laceration proximally and distally to fully evaluate the extent of the soft-tissue injury. All
devitalized muscle, fascia, and bone should be excised, and the wound must be irrigated
with the use of an appropriate volume of sterile saline. Before wound closure, the open
wound can be used for plafond reduction and fixation if the treating surgeon believes
the open wound has been thoroughly débrided and is clean enough to accept implants.
This may be particularly valuable in patients who have a plafond fracture with tension
failure along the medial distal tibia.
For surgeons planning to definitively manage the tibial plafond injury, fibular fixation
during the initial stage is associated with several advantages. Anatomic fibular fixation
helps restore lower limb length and may aid in indirect reduction of the Chaput and/or
Volkmann fragments via ligamentotaxis. Fibular fixation affords additional coronal
stability to a tibial plafond fracture that has been provisionally placed in an external

and anterior (Figures 32 and 33). To adequately visualize the posterior joint, joint
distraction can be performed with the use of a femoral distractor or a spanning external
fixator. If a femoral distractor is selected, a Schanz pin can be placed into the tibia and
the talar neck from medial or lateral, depending on the surgical approach. Specifically,
Volkmann fragment reduction is maintained and verified via fluoroscopy, after which
transosseous Kirschner wire fixation is performed percutaneously through the fibula or
through the exposed tibia and into the Volkmann fragment. The section of central
marginal impaction is then mobilized and reduced. The subchondral bone must be left
attached to the articular surface, and the entire segment must be mobilized as a unit.
After marginal impaction is reduced and pinned in place, a void is present behind the
fragment. The void is sufficiently filled with cancellous allograft, local bone autograft, or
calcium phosphate bone substitute.

Standard principles for the management of intra-articular fractures apply.
Definitive joint-spanning external fixation with limited internal fixation has been described and
has been reported to result in out­comes similar to those of ORIF.

wires at the joint surface). They are not as stable as circular external fixation.

maintained circumferentially, and future swelling must be considered.

orthogonally to the tibial shaft close to the proximal fracture line. The stable base is attached
to the tibial shaft with the use of 5-mm hydroxyapatite-coated half pins.
The floating ring is positioned between the stable base and the foot ring.

the articular ring to increase stability.

fracture is then distracted. This restores length and allows for the eventual reduction of the
articular surface via a limited open technique.
Limited anterior and occasional posterolateral approaches are used to expose and reduce and
stabilize the articular fragments.

bioabsorbable pins, and small rim plates. Anatomic reduction always is the goal.

reduction. It also allows for the use of less fluoroscopy.

fracture fragments through small skin incisions.

Techniques
Circular external fixation is a skill acquired through intensive training. Many of the
techniques described in this section have been adapted from those described by Hutson
Jr.37 Attention to detail during every step is important to prevent a poorly placed frame
and a poorly reduced fracture. Simply placing rings around the ankle will not lead to a
good result. Radiolucent carbon fiber rings are used to allow for visualization of the
fracture fragments. The first step is to select the correct ring size. This depends on the
size of the patient, the amount of swelling at the time of surgical management, and the
expected amount of postoperative swelling. Ring size can be selected at the time of
definitive surgical management. The frame does not have to be pre-built; it can be
rapidly assembled as assistants prepare and drape the patient. After the temporary
external fixator is removed, rings between 160 and 180 mm are brought up over the
tibia. At least two fingerbreadths of clearance must be maintained circumferentially. The
closer the rings are to the patient, observing this rule, the more stable the fixation.
The next step is to bring the assembled frame over the leg. The frame consists of two
rings forming the stable base, a floating ring for later metaphyseal fixation, and the foot
ring (Figure 40). The stable base is attached to the tibial shaft in an orthogonal manner.
This means that it is attached parallel to the long axis of the leg in the coronal and
sagittal planes. The distal ring of the stable base is brought as close to the fracture as
possible to increase stability. The first point of fixation is an anterior to posterior 5-mm
hydroxyapatite-coated half pin placed off the distal ring of the stable base. It is attached
to the ring with the use of a rancho cube constructed in a manner that allows for
rotation of the frame in multiple planes. The second point of fixation is another anterior
to posterior 5-mm half pin placed off the proximal ring of the stable base. The stable
base is then aligned parallel to the tibia in the anteroposterior and lateral planes. After
aligned orthogonally to the tibia, reduction of the fracture is easier. Additional fixation of
the stable base is placed after the remaining external fixation is completed.

Postoperative Management
Postoperative management after the application of an external fixator consists of pin
care, wound care, and swelling prevention. No pin care is administered for the first week
postoperatively. The sponges that are placed around each pin are left in situ and are
changed only if they are bloody. After 1 week, the pins are cleansed with the use of soap
and water or saline every other day. The main goal is to remove any dried fluids. The
sponges are changed only if soiled. They are pressed gently against the skin and held in
place with the use of a clip. This prevents pistoning and skin irritation, which decrease
the risk of pin site infection. More frequent pin care has been associated with increased
infection risk. Standard surgical wound care is performed. The dressings are not
disturbed for 2 weeks postoperatively unless they are soiled. The sutures are not
removed until the wound is completely healed. This usually occurs 2 to 3 weeks
postoperatively.

Nonunion
Nonunion rates after ORIF of tibial plafond fractures are range from 2% to 25%. In the
largest series of more than 500 patients with a tibial plafond fracture, Haller et al33
reported a nonunion rate of 14%. Several risk factors for nonunion have been identified,
including open fracture, bone loss, associated compartment syndrome, associated
fibular fracture, and tobacco use. The use of multiple surgical approaches has a
conflicting association with nonunion.33,38,39 Several surgeon-related factors, including
the use of locking plates and lack of medial column support, also have been associated
with an increased rate of nonunion.33 Failure to include a medial-sided implant is
associated with higher nonunion rates for varus and valgus failure tibial plafond
fractures.33
Most tibial plafond nonunions occur in the metadiaphysis, and articular nonunion is
rare. Patients should undergo standard nonunion evaluation, including examination of
surrounding soft tissue, CT evaluation of the osseous healing, and laboratory evaluation
for infectious or metabolic factors.40 Given that most nonunions involve the metaphysis
or metadiaphysis, revision surgery should focus on restoring length, alignment, and
rotation of the tibia with consideration for bone grafting. After correction of these
factors, definitive fixation can proceed with the use of a plate, nail, or external fixator.33

Infection
Infection after tibial plafond fracture may be a devastating complication that is
potentially limb-threatening and requires urgent surgical management. Before staged
management, deep infection was reported to occur in as many as 50% of patients with a
tibial plafond fracture who underwent ORIF.42-44 Staged management and modern
advances in soft-tissue handling, surgical approaches, and anatomic plates have led to a
substantial reduction in the rate of postoperative infection. Using modern techniques,
recent studies have reported infection rates between 2% and 19%.21,45-47
Unsurprisingly, patients with diabetes mellitus and patients with a Gustilo-Anderson
grade III fracture have a substantially higher risk for postoperative infection.45,47 In
additions, patients who have a fracture with segmental bone loss have a higher risk for
infection, likely because of the energy of the injury.45 Despite concerns regarding the
tenuous medial soft-tissue envelope, surgical approach does not appear to be
associated with postoperative infection.45,46
Patients with a tibial plafond fracture who have a postoperative infection should
undergo surgical débridement in a timely fashion. After all infected and devitalized tissue
has been excised and intraoperative tissue cultures have been obtained, the wound
should be thoroughly irrigated with the use of normal saline. Implants that are required
for stability should remain in place or be exchanged because fracture stability is
paramount to clearing a deep surgical site infection. Intrawound antibiotic powder or
antibiotic-eluting calcium sulfate or polymethyl methacrylate can be used to locally
increase the minimum inhibitory concentration to minimize bacterial recolonization.48-50
Devitalized skin edges should be excised to optimize wound healing and avoid prolonged
closure. Patients should be treated via prolonged antibiotic therapy guided by
intraoperative tissue culture results.


External Fixation
Infection complications unique to external fixation exist. Pin site infections are rare after
the application of temporary pin-to-bar external fixators. Contributing factors include
burning the bone during the placement of the external fixation pins and leaving bony
debris at the pin site. To decrease the risk of infection, predrilling of the pin sites is
helpful. If using self-drilling pins, drill them in slowly, and use saline to cool the pin.
During placement of the tibial pins, do not enter the bone through the tibial crest, which
has the thickest and hardest bone.
Infection complications unique to definitive fixation include those already mentioned but
also include the prolonged nature of the use of the frame. Pin site infections are
common if a frame is used for months. To decrease the risk of infection at the pin sites,
sponges or gauze should be placed around the pins to prevent pistoning and skin
irritation. The pins should be cleaned with the use of soap and water or saline every
other day to remove debris. Use of hydroxyapatite-coated half pins leads to better bone
fixation and, therefore, fewer pin site infections. To prevent deep infections and septic
arthritis, olive wires should not be allowed to contact the limited internal fixation, and
the wires should not be placed closer than 1 cm to the joint surface, respectively.51
If a pin site infection occurs, the patient should be treated via a brief course of an oral
antibiotic with appropriate gram-positive coverage. Cultures of the pin site drainage
should be obtained, and antibiotic agents should be adjusted based on final culture
results and response to initial management. The antibiotic agent is continued until the
pin site infection resolves. If the infection is not better after approximately 1 week, the
patient can be admitted to the hospital and treated via intravenous antibiotic agents. If
the infection does not resolve, then the wire or pin should be removed, and a new wire
or pin should be placed.

Other Complications
Ankle arthritis
Substantial arthrosis of the ankle joint is com­mon after tibial plafond fracture.
One study reported, arthrosis in 74% of patients 5 to 11 years postinjury.
Arthrosis most commonly begins within 1 or 2 years postinjury.
Radiographic arthritis does not always correlate with subjective clinical results. Despite the
devastating effects to the articular surface and the problems associated with fracture of the
tibial plafond, arthrodesis is not commonly required until many years postinjury.

Other Complications
Posttraumatic osteoarthritis of the ankle (PTOA) is common after tibial plafond fracture.
Tibial plafond fractures result in some of the highest rates of PTOA. Studies show that
ankle arthrosis may occur in 40% of patients at 2 years postinjury and 74% of patients at
a minimum of 5 years postinjury.53,54 Studies have demonstrated that even 3 years
postinjury, patients continue to have poor outcomes that affect health and quality of life
compared with age-matched controls; this may be the beginning of a lifetime of
impairment.7 Despite advances in health care and fracture management, the incidence
of PTOA after intra-articular fracture has remained relatively unchanged in the past few
decades.

Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation after tibial plafond fracture is pro¬longed. Patients should be counseled that
weight bearing may be delayed for 3 months or more.
In patients treated via external fixation, healing time generally is 12 to 16 weeks.
Tibial plafond fractures have a substantial, deleterious long-term effect on ankle function and
quality of life. Poorer outcomes are observed in patients in whom complications occur.
If possible, ankle joint motion should be permitted and facilitated.
The use of a removable boot or brace may be beneficial as the patient transitions from
immobilization and non–weight bearing to mobilization and protected–weight bearing.
Definitive External Fixation

Definitive External Fixation
Features unique to definitive external fixation include the possibility of early weight
bearing and early functional activity. The principles of external fixation include relative
stability. Therefore, all patients except those with a highly comminuted fracture are
encouraged to bear weight early after the placement of a circular external fixation
system. During the phase of joint spanning, usually the first 6 weeks postoperatively,
patients can bear as much weight as tolerated; however, the olive wires in the foot often
will cause some discomfort, leading to self-limitation on weight bearing. If the articular
surface fixation is deemed to be stable after removal of the foot frame, patients can
rapidly proceed to weight-bearing ambulation as tolerated. Activities such as walking in a
clean, chlorinated pool are encouraged. Patients with a circular frame are encouraged to
normalize activities as soon as feasible. Physical therapy should be initiated as early as
possible to improve range of motion of the foot and ankle. This usually begins after
removal of the foot ring at 6 weeks postoperatively.

Overall Outcomes
High-energy tibial pilon fractures are severe injuries that lead to considerable functional
decline, chronic pain, and deterioration of quality of life. Different outcomes are
observed with different methods of definitive management; however, no treatment
methods are capable of producing optimal results in all patients.
In 2003, Pollak et al7 published a study demonstrating the devastating consequences of
tibial pilon fractures, including high percentages of patients with stiffness, swelling,
chronic pain, and inability to work. The authors reported numerous factors that led to a
suboptimal outcome, including lower socioeconomic status, marriage, and multiple
comorbidities. Fractures managed via external fixation were associated with poorer
outcomes but included fractures with more severe soft-tissue injuries.
De-Las-Heras-Romero et al59 reported that pilon fractures have a dramatic effect on
quality of life. The effect is influenced by the severity of the injury, the accuracy of
reduction, and the development of posttraumatic arthrosis.
In 2019, Foster et al60 demonstrated that patients with associated mental health
disorders have higher complication rates, higher hospital readmission rates, and higher
revision surgery rates.

Pearls and Pitfalls
Temporary Pin-to-Bar External Fixation

Understand the local anatomy to avoid neurovascular or tendon injury.
Pre-drill pin sites or use saline and slow drilling to prevent burning and subsequent

Keep working length as short as possible to enhance stability.

Use medial and lateral bars.
Keep pin sites away from sites at which definitive hardware will be placed.

Burning the bone during the placement of the tibial pins leads to a ring sequestrum.

Placing the first metatarsal pin in the soft, proximal metaphyseal bone may lead to loss of

A long working length leads to instability at the fracture site.
